subject: maths
title: Triangles
summary: Classifying triangles by sides and angles, and using the angle sum of 180° and the exterior angle rule to find missing angles.
body:
A **triangle** is a flat shape with three straight sides. Triangles are everywhere in building — roof trusses, bridges and bike frames all use triangles because a triangle cannot be squashed out of shape. In this lesson you will name the different types of triangle and use the angle sum to find missing angles.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can classify triangles by their sides and angles, and use the facts that the angles in a triangle add to 180° and an exterior angle equals the two opposite interior angles.

## Before you start

You need Measuring and classifying angles (Year 7) and Angles and parallel lines (Year 7) — especially angles on a straight line adding to 180° and alternate angles being equal.

**Warm-up**

1. Work out 180 − (60 + 75).
2. Is an angle of 95° acute or obtuse?

*Answers:* 1. 45 2. obtuse

## Think of it like this

### Tearing off the corners

Draw any triangle on paper and cut it out. Tear off the three corners and line them up side by side, points touching. However you drew the triangle — tall, flat, lopsided — the three corners always fit together to make a **straight line**. That is why the three angles of a triangle add to 180°.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* tearing paper is a demonstration, not a proof — it only shows it works for the triangles you tried. The parallel-line reason below shows it works for every triangle.

## Key ideas

### Naming triangles by their sides

- **Equilateral** — all three sides equal. All three angles are equal too (60° each).
- **Isosceles** — two sides equal. The two angles opposite the equal sides (the **base angles**) are equal.
- **Scalene** — no sides equal, and no angles equal.

Equal sides are shown with matching dash marks on a diagram.

![An equilateral triangle ABC with one dash mark on each side, showing all three sides are equal](/diagrams/y7/maths/triangles-equilateral.svg)

### Naming triangles by their angles

- **Acute-angled** — all three angles are acute.
- **Right-angled** — one angle is 90°.
- **Obtuse-angled** — one angle is obtuse.

A triangle can have both kinds of name, for example a "right-angled isosceles triangle".

### The angle sum of a triangle is 180°

The three **interior angles** (the angles inside) of any triangle add to 180°.

Why? Draw a line through the top corner, parallel to the bottom side. The angle at the top sits between two angles on that straight line. Each of those is an alternate angle to one of the bottom corners, so they are equal. The three angles on the straight line add to 180°, and they are exactly the three angles of the triangle.

### The exterior angle

If you extend one side of a triangle past a corner, the angle between the extended line and the next side is an **exterior angle**. The exterior angle equals the **sum of the two interior opposite angles** (the two angles not next to it).

Why? The exterior angle and the interior angle next to it make 180° (a straight line). The three interior angles also make 180°. So the exterior angle must equal the other two interior angles added together.

### Which triangles are possible?

Because the angles add to 180°, a triangle can have at most one right angle or one obtuse angle. Two right angles would already use up 180°, leaving nothing for the third corner.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

A triangle has angles 50°, 70° and a°. Find a.

![Triangle ABC with angle A = 50°, angle B = 70° and angle C marked a](/diagrams/y7/maths/triangles-ex1.svg)

Step 1: Angles in a triangle add to 180°.
Step 2: Add the known angles: 50 + 70 = 120.
Step 3: a = 180 − 120 = 60.
Check: 50 + 70 + 60 = 180 ✓

### Example 2

A right-angled triangle has one other angle of 35°. Find the third angle.

![Right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at A, angle B = 35° and angle C marked with a question mark](/diagrams/y7/maths/triangles-ex2.svg)

Step 1: One angle is 90° — it is a right-angled triangle.
Step 2: 90 + 35 = 125 — add the known angles.
Step 3: 180 − 125 = 55, so the third angle is 55°.
Check: 90 + 35 + 55 = 180 ✓

### Example 3

An isosceles triangle has an angle of 40° between its two equal sides. Find the two base angles.

![Isosceles triangle ABC with equal sides CA and CB marked with dashes, a 40° angle at C, and both base angles at A and B marked with question marks](/diagrams/y7/maths/triangles-ex3.svg)

Step 1: The base angles are equal — that is the isosceles rule.
Step 2: The base angles together make 180 − 40 = 140 — angle sum.
Step 3: Each base angle is 140 ÷ 2 = 70°.
Check: 40 + 70 + 70 = 180 ✓

### Example 4

A triangle has interior angles of 62° and 48°. The side next to the third angle is extended to make an exterior angle. Find the exterior angle.

![Triangle ABC with angle A = 62° and angle C = 48°; side AB is extended past B and the exterior angle at B is marked with a question mark](/diagrams/y7/maths/triangles-ex4.svg)

Step 1: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
Step 2: 62 + 48 = 110, so the exterior angle is 110°.
Check: the third interior angle is 180 − 110 = 70, and 70 + 110 = 180 on the straight line ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Using 360° for a triangle.** 360° is for angles at a point and for quadrilaterals. Fix: three angles, half a turn, 180°.
- **Choosing the wrong base angles in an isosceles triangle.** The equal angles are opposite the equal sides, not at the ends of them. Fix: find the odd side (the base) — the equal angles sit on either end of it.
- **Adding the wrong angles for an exterior angle.** Fix: add the two angles that are *not* next to the exterior angle.
- **Thinking a scalene triangle can have equal angles.** Fix: no equal sides means no equal angles.

## Tips to remember

- **"Tri-180":** three corners, torn off, make a straight line. Picture the torn paper corners. (Made-up memory trick.)
- **Isosceles = "I-SOS-celes" — "Same Opposite Sides"**: two equal sides give two equal angles opposite them. (Made-up memory trick.)
- **Equilateral = "equal lateral"** — "lateral" means sides, so all sides equal.
- **Scalene sounds like "scaly"** — bumpy and uneven, nothing matches.
- **Exterior angle = "the far two"** — add the two corners far from it.

## Key terms

- **Triangle** — a flat shape with three straight sides.
- **Interior angle** — an angle inside a shape at a corner.
- **Equilateral triangle** — all sides and all angles equal (each angle 60°).
- **Isosceles triangle** — two equal sides and two equal base angles.
- **Scalene triangle** — no equal sides or angles.
- **Right-angled, acute-angled, obtuse-angled** — triangles named by their largest angle.
- **Exterior angle** — the angle between one side and the extension of the next side.

## Summary

- Triangles are named by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse).
- The angles in a triangle add to 180°.
- In an isosceles triangle the base angles are equal; in an equilateral triangle each angle is 60°.
- An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
- A triangle can have at most one right or obtuse angle.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles of 65°, 45° and x°. Find x.
questions.explanation: The angles in a triangle add to 180°: 65 + 45 = 110 and 180 − 110 = 70. 250 comes from using 360°.
steps: Angles in a triangle add to 180°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 110 is the total of the known angles — subtract it from 180.
mistakes.C: Step 1: angles in a triangle add to 180°, not 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A = 65°, angle B = 45° and angle C marked x

questions.prompt: A triangle has exactly two equal sides. What type of triangle is it?
questions.explanation: A triangle with exactly two equal sides is isosceles. Equilateral needs all three sides equal.
steps: Count the equal sides: there are two.
Three equal sides = equilateral; no equal sides = scalene.

mistakes.A: Step 2: equilateral needs ALL three sides equal.
mistakes.B: Step 2: scalene means NO equal sides.
mistakes.D: Step 1: right-angled is about having a 90° angle, not about equal sides.

questions.prompt: What size is each angle in an equilateral triangle?
questions.explanation: All three angles are equal and add to 180°, so each is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. 90° would be a right angle, which can't happen three times in a triangle.
steps: In an equilateral triangle all three angles are equal.

mistakes.A: Step 2: three right angles would add to 270°, but triangles only have 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 180° is the total of all three angles — share it between them.

questions.prompt: A right-angled triangle has another angle of 28°. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: The angles add to 180°: 90 + 28 = 118 and 180 − 118 = 62°. 152° forgets the right angle (180 − 28).

mistakes.B: Step 1: don't forget the right angle — it is 90° and must be included.
mistakes.D: Step 3: the third angle doesn't have to equal 28° — that's only for isosceles triangles.

questions.diagram_alt: Right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at A, angle B = 28° and angle C marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: An isosceles triangle has an angle of 50° between its two equal sides. What size is each base angle?
questions.explanation: The base angles share 180 − 50 = 130°, so each is 65°. 80° comes from making a base angle 50° by mistake and finding the angle at the top.
steps: The base angles are the two equal angles.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the 50° angle is between the equal sides, so it is NOT a base angle.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you treated 50° as a base angle. It is the angle between the equal sides.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 130° is shared between TWO base angles — divide by 2.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles triangle ABC with equal sides CA and CB marked with dashes, a 50° angle at C, and the base angles at A and B marked with question marks

questions.prompt: A triangle has interior angles of 52° and 71°. What is the exterior angle at the third corner?
questions.explanation: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles: 52 + 71 = 123°. 57° is the third interior angle, not the exterior one.
steps: The exterior angle at the third corner is opposite the 52° and 71° angles.
Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 180 − 123 = 57° is the INTERIOR angle at that corner; the exterior angle is next to it.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the exterior angle is 52 + 71; don't subtract from 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with interior angles 52° at A and 71° at C; side AB is extended past B and the exterior angle at B is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: An isosceles triangle has base angles of 50° each. What is the third angle, and what type of triangle is it by angles?
questions.explanation: 180 − (50 + 50) = 80°, and all three angles (50°, 50°, 80°) are acute, so it is acute-angled. 130° comes from subtracting only one base angle.
steps: The two base angles are 50° and 50°.
All angles are less than 90°, so it is acute-angled.

mistakes.B: Step 2: subtract BOTH base angles (50 + 50), not just one.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 80° is less than 90°, so it is acute, not obtuse.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 50° is a base angle, not the top angle — (180 − 50) ÷ 2 treats it the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: The angles of a triangle are x°, 2x° and 3x°. Find the largest angle.
questions.explanation: x + 2x + 3x = 6x = 180, so x = 30 and the largest angle is 3 × 30 = 90°. 30° is x itself, the smallest angle.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 30° is x, the smallest angle. The largest is 3x.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 60° is 2x, the middle angle. The largest is 3x.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 180 is the total of all the angles — find x first, then 3x.

questions.prompt: An exterior angle of a triangle is 130°. One interior opposite angle is 75°. Find the other interior opposite angle.
questions.explanation: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles: 75 + ? = 130, so the missing angle is 130 − 75 = 55°. 50° is the interior angle next to the exterior angle (180 − 130).
steps: Exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 180 − 130 = 50° is the interior angle NEXT to the exterior angle, not an opposite one.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you did 180 − 75, as if 75° were on a straight line with something. Use the exterior angle rule: 75 + missing angle = 130.
mistakes.C: Step 3: subtract 75 from 130 — don't add them.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with side AB extended past B; the exterior angle at B is 130°, the interior angle at A is 75° and the interior angle at C is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Mia says a triangle can have two obtuse angles if they are both only just over 90°. Which statement explains why she is wrong?

options.A: Two angles over 90° add to more than 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle
options.B: Obtuse angles can only appear in quadrilaterals
options.C: A triangle needs at least one right angle
options.D: Two obtuse angles would add to exactly 180°

questions.explanation: Two angles each over 90° add to more than 180°, but the three angles must total exactly 180°, so it is impossible. Saying they add to exactly 180° is wrong, because each is more than 90°.
steps: The three angles must add to exactly 180°.
Two angles each bigger than 90° add to more than 180°.
That leaves no room (a negative amount) for the third angle, so it's impossible.

mistakes.B: Step 1: triangles can have one obtuse angle — the problem is having two.
mistakes.C: Step 1: many triangles have no right angle at all, e.g. 60°, 60°, 60°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: each is MORE than 90°, so together they are more than 180°, not exactly 180°.

questions.prompt: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the largest angle?
questions.explanation: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts make 180°, so one part is 20° and the largest angle is 4 × 20° = 80°. 160° comes from sharing 360° instead of 180°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 40° is the smallest angle (2 parts). The largest is 4 parts.
mistakes.B: Step 1: angles in a triangle add to 180°, not 360°.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 60° is the middle angle (3 parts). The largest is 4 parts.

questions.prompt: In triangle PQR, PQ = PR and angle Q = 72°. Side QR is extended past R to point S. Find angle PRS.
questions.explanation: PQ = PR, so the base angles Q and R are equal: angle PRQ = 72°. Angle PRS is on a straight line with it: 180 − 72 = 108°. 72° stops at the interior angle.
steps: PQ = PR, so the triangle is isosceles and the angles opposite those sides (R and Q) are equal: angle PRQ = 72°.
Q, R and S are on a straight line, so angle PRS + angle PRQ = 180°.
Angle PRS = 180 − 72 = 108° (check: angle P = 36° and 36 + 72 = 108 ✓ exterior angle rule).

mistakes.B: Step 2: 72° is the interior angle PRQ. Angle PRS is the exterior angle next to it.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 36° is angle P at the top. You need the exterior angle at R.
mistakes.D: Step 1: angle R equals angle Q (72°) — you doubled 72° instead of using the straight line.
